highlights.text: gives its core meaning as: piercing or jabbing into something with an implement that goes through it
ṭaʿantu fī al-rajuli ṭaʿanānan ("I reviled the man")
uses ṭaʿanān for reviling: "the manifestness of enmity insists on nothing but ... reviling, and saying what should not be said."
Ibn Fāris supports this with a ḥadīth: "the believer is not a ṭaʿʿān"
a single authentic root meaning the circling of one thing around another, and a thing's being surrounded or encompassed
طُوفَان (ṭūfān) — a flood: water that circles around things and envelops them
in the Arabic language proper, any group able to encircle a thing is a ṭāʾifa
a line of al-Aʿshā describing a jinn-sent frenzy (awlaq)
jurists and exegetes variously make it four-or-more, or three, or even a single person
a sound minor root with two different meanings: certainty and doubt
ẓanantu ẓannan can mean "I was certain."
ẓanantu al-shayʾ: to hold something without being certain of it.
Al-Nābighah: "the maẓinnah of folly is youth."
a single root meaning: the scattering of a thing and making it manifest
The Qur'an has "and carpets mabthūtha" (Q 88:16), which Ibn Fāris glosses as "many and spread about."
The Qur'an quotes one who said, "I only complain of my bathth and my grief to God" (Q 12:86).
Al-Nābigha describes a hunter who "loosed them in all directions upon it,"
one sound root meaning a splitting or cleaving-apart in something
The language scholars derive the word for "poor man" (faqīr) from this — as though he were someone with a broken backbone, because of his lowliness and abjectness.
al-fāqira = a disaster; "the fāqira struck them,"
illustrated by a verse hoping in the Lord "for the stopping-up of my points of need."
something getting caught/entangled/stuck fast within something else
أَغْلَقْتُ الْبَابَ = "I locked/shut the door"; it is then mughlaq ("locked").
Zuhayr's line about a woman parting with an unredeemable pledge on the day of farewell, "so the pledge became ghaliqā [forfeited]."
"with locking arrows [maghāliq] of matching shape."
Ibn Fāris cites a saying attributed to the Prophet: "The pledge does not become forfeited" (لَا يَغْلَقُ الرَّهْنُ).
The organizing idea is covering / veiling, from which the other senses branch.
highlights.note: the editor's summary of the root sense

highlights.text: غمّ (ghamma) is to distress or oppress.
To be فِي غمّة (fī ghumma) of one's affair is to be in a perplexity from which one sees no way out.
"She smiles showing teeth like ḥabb al-ghamām"
He splits the root into two independent bases
**الغَيّ (al-ghayy)**: the opposite of *rushd* (right guidance) — ignorance of a matter and sinking into falsehood.
Verb غَوَى / يَغْوِي (ghawā/yaghwī, "to go astray").
Illustrated by a line of verse contrasting the man praised for meeting good with the one who "goes astray" and never lacks a blamer.
glosses jufāʾ as what a flood-torrent (wādī) or a cooking-pot throws off to its sides: the floating scum/debris (ghuthāʾ) that gets cast aside as worthless.
He cites 13:17 — "But as for the scum, it goes away as jufāʾ"
Bringing a thing from one place to another
A covering that coats something (الْجُلْبَة)
From this covering-sense comes الْجِلْبَاب, "the shirt/wrap" (plural جَلَابِيب).
A cited verse compares vultures walking calmly in an open, threat-free space to young women walking about wrapped in their jalālīb
الْجَلَب is a specific practice condemned in a hadith
a single root whose branches all return to one core idea: cutting or severing (al-qaṭʿ)
الجُرم and الجَريمة mean a sin (dhanb).
He explains the expression لا جَرَمَ (lā jarama) likewise as coming from jaramtu ("I earned")
citing a verse where a spear-thrust "earned" the tribe Fazāra their anger
a single sound root meaning the opposite of truthfulness
al-kadhib is the opposite of al-ṣidq (truthfulness): kadhaba kadhiban ("he lied").
kadhdhabtu fulānan = I accused him of lying / gave him the lie
Intensive forms for a habitual liar: kadhdhāb and kudhaba.
Ibn Fāris cites Abū Duʾād on a wild ass that "lied" (held back) even though it did rush.
a sound root which, he says, indicates gathering and being gathered together
kababtu al-shayʾa li-wajhihi, "I threw the thing down on its face"
akabba ʿalā al-amr: a man "bends over" a matter he is doing.
Al-Aʿshā describes a glistening blossom (kawkab) that "smiles back at the sun", wrapped about with luxuriant growth.
a single, sound root whose core meaning is: a person going around / circling close to something, seeking shelter in it and using it as cover
Form III — لَاوَذَ (lāwadha), verbal noun liwādh, "to take shelter one behind another."
He explains this described the hypocrites: when one of them wanted to leave the Prophet's gathering, he would duck behind someone else to hide himself before slipping off.
a core idea of "cutting off a portion,"
God bestowed favor on His servants; He is al-Mannān (the great Bestower).
al-manūn is "the cutter," equated with al-maniyyah (death).
ajr ghayr mamnūn is placed here — "a reward not cut off / undiminished."
Aws praises a rope "tightly twisted, not worn out (ghayr manīn)."
a benefit, and the extension of a good period of time
He cites Q 24:29, "uninhabited houses in which there is matāʿ [benefit] for you."
From it comes istamtaʿtu bi-l-shayʾ ("I got benefit/enjoyment out of the thing").
God kept someone alive so as to benefit from him in joys and advantages
mātiʿ (of a "balance") is glossed as rājiḥ zāʾid — "outweighing, surpassing."
from two distinct bases
"nakifa min al-amr" and "istankafa minhu" mean he disdained something — regarded it as beneath him
an Arab saying describes a rainstorm so persistent that "no one could nakafahu" (cut it short) even over a day or two
a single sound root meaning debasement and putting to death
قَتَلَهُ قَتْلًا (he killed him).
He cites Q 4:157 {وما قتلوه يقينًا} in this sense — "they did not attain sure knowledge of it."
with Imruʾ al-Qays's line about arrows striking "the pieces of a slain heart."
a single root whose core idea is setting out and going forward on a journey
رَحَلَ / يَرْحَلُ / رِحْلَة — to travel, a journeying.
properly it names the traveller's equipment that goes with him, which he loads up when he moves on and returns to when he halts
a single, consistent core meaning: al-ittibāʿ, "the following of a thing" — one thing coming after another
al-tarāduf — succession, one thing after another.
"A matter befell them, then something greater ridifa [followed] it" — the second event outweighing the first.
In Labīd's poetry, al-ridf names a ship's steersman.
سُنْبُل (sunbul) is the ear or head of a standing crop; plural سَنابِل, singulative سُنْبُلَة (one ear).
Reported of Salmān, seen at Kūfa wearing a قميص سُنْبُلانيّ.
one consistent root meaning: the flowing of a thing and its running on with ease
al-sunna is al-sīra, a way of conduct or course followed
mud that seems to have been poured out.
The sinn (tooth) of a person or animal is likened to a spearhead.
"do not be distressed at a sunna you yourself set going; the first to accept a sunna is the one who sets it going."
going forth freely, moving off without being held back (al-inṭilāq)
سَرَّحْتُ الْمَرْأَةَ = "I let the woman go."
He cites Q 2:231, {أَوْ سَرِّحُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ} ("or release them in a fitting manner").
السَّرْح (al-sarḥ): livestock turned out to pasture.
a line of ʿAntara describing a champion whose garments hang as if on a sarḥah-tree
(1) a thing rising up or bursting forth
(2) a kind of animal
ثَارَ (thāra), imperfect yathūru, with three verbal nouns — thawr, thuʾūr, thawarān: a thing rises up, stirs, breaks out.
a trace or impression (athar) left as a distinguishing mark (maʿlam)
wasamtu al-shayʾa wasman, "I marked it"
glosses al-mutawassimīn simply as "those who look for the telling/indicative mark"
at dawn they were like graceful doom-palms, moving in the direction taken by a departing traveler who reads the tracks (mutawassim).
